title: Freshworks Alumni Raise $53 Million for Dreamteam, an AI-Native CRM Challenger
excerpt: Anand Venkatraman, Senthil Kanthaswamy and Ramesh Parthasarathy have closed a Together Fund-led seed and an Accel-led Series A for a CRM whose records maintain themselves — with engineering in Chennai and more than 100 customers signed in three months of selling.
body:
• Dreamteam, an AI-native CRM startup founded in 2025 by three former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million across a seed round led by Together Fund and a Series A led by Accel, with Premji Invest participating.
  • Its CRM replaces manual data entry with a "Company Brain" that builds a living record from emails and meetings, plus four built-in AI agents handling research, meeting preparation, pipeline monitoring and system administration.
  • The California-based company, whose engineering team is in Chennai, says it signed more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling, most of them paying. It declined to disclose its valuation or the size of each round.

Three alumni of Freshworks, the Chennai-founded software company, have raised $53 million to build a customer relationship management platform designed for AI agents first and human data entry second. Dreamteam, founded in 2025, announced the funding on November 16 across two rounds: a seed round led by Together Fund and a Series A led by Accel, with Premji Invest participating, according to TechCrunch. The company declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

The founders' complaint with CRM

Co-founder and chief executive Anand Venkatraman spent more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks, and told TechCrunch he had repeatedly encountered the same problem: salespeople spent considerable time updating CRM records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their pipeline. His co-founders are Senthil Kanthaswamy, who spent more than nine years at Freshworks and was most recently a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy, who worked on AI and platform engineering there. The company's announcement says the three helped scale Freshworks from its early startup days through its IPO. The company is based in California with go-to-market operations in the United States and its engineering team in Chennai, and employs more than 35 people.

"We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record."

— Anand Venkatraman, co-founder and CEO, Dreamteam, to TechCrunch

What the product does

Dreamteam's pitch is that the record should maintain itself. At the centre of the product is what the company calls the Company Brain, a shared memory assembled from emails, meetings and other customer interactions, which the announcement says captures buyer intent, objections, competitor mentions and stakeholder dynamics. On top of it sit four built-in AI agents: Rachel, which researches and enriches accounts and contacts; Sally, a sales assistant that prepares users for meetings, drafts follow-up emails and manages tasks; Raj, a RevOps partner that monitors pipelines, flags deal risks and works on forecasting; and Alex, a CRM administrator that sets up and maintains the system. A feature called Magic Apps lets users create custom applications and dashboards inside the CRM using natural-language instructions, without code. Sales teams retain control over what is sent to customers and review proposed actions before they go out. The company says it plans to expand beyond sales into onboarding, customer support and upselling.

Early traction, stated carefully

Venkatraman told TechCrunch the company signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service. Named wins include replacing Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and replacing HubSpot at other customers; the advertising sales team at streaming company Plex chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native alternatives. Current revenue was not disclosed; Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, and believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers fully adapt to AI. Together Fund, Dreamteam's first institutional investor, was founded by Girish Mathrubootham — himself the founder of Freshworks — who said, in the company's announcement coverage, that "CRM is among the biggest software categories ripe for disruption." Accel partner Shekhar Kirani described the opportunity as redefining what the announcement calls the $100B+ CRM market. Readers can find the product at dreamteam.ai.

The counter-argument

The incumbents are not standing still, and TechCrunch notes the sceptical case: in a blog post earlier this year, Andreessen Horowitz argued that existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them rather than replacing them. Venkatraman acknowledged Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon. What to watch next is whether Dreamteam's early displacements — a healthcare company off Salesforce, a media sales team off HubSpot — multiply into the kind of installed base that survives the incumbents' own AI releases, and whether the company discloses revenue or a valuation when it next raises.
